sentences.text: Gilmoreosaurus was a large hadrosauroid that could reach lengths of up to 6.2 meters and weigh between 1.2 and 3.6 tons.
Although no complete articulated skull is known, numerous elements including the maxilla, dentary, jugal, squamosal, lacrimals, quadrate, and predentary have been discovered.
Its teeth were oval-shaped with a pinched upper end and coarse denticles possessing three diminutive pointed structures.
The genus Gilmoreosaurus was formally described by Brett-Surman in 1979.
The species originally named Mandschurosaurus mongoliensis was later reclassified as the type species Gilmoreosaurus mongoliensis.
The type species is known from the Iren Dabasu Formation in Inner Mongolia and dates to 96 million years ago.
Additional species G. atavus and G. arkhangelskyi have been described from Uzbekistan, but their classification is considered dubious due to fragmentary remains.
The species G. kysylkumense is sometimes included in Gilmoreosaurus but has also been referred to the genus Bactrosaurus.
Many consider Gilmoreosaurus one of the most primitive hadrosaurids, characterized by large lower jaws, long hind legs, and the absence of a hollow crest.
The tooth row in Gilmoreosaurus is oriented to the lateral sides, a trait seen in hadrosauroids but lost in more advanced hadrosaurids.
A ridge-like formation on the posterior edge of the quadrate is reported in other iguanodontians and hadrosauroids like Brachylophosaurus and Gryposaurus.
The bottom tilt of the lateral malleolus is a trait used to distinguish juvenile from adult tibiae in Gilmoreosaurus.
Brett-Surman described Gilmoreosaurus anatomy as partly iguanodont and partly hadrosaurine, viewing it as an ancestral hadrosaurine form.
The idea that the two Iren Dabasu hadrosaurs were synonyms was rejected due to numerous differences found between them.
Gilmoreosaurus lived from the Aptian to Campanian stages of the Middle to Late Cretaceous, approximately 120 to 70 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
Specifically, Gilmoreosaurus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
Anatoly K. Rozhdestvensky debated in the 1960s that Bactrosaurus was a hadrosaurine rather than a lambeosaurine.
Later authors disagreed with Rozhdestvensky, maintaining that Bactrosaurus is a lambeosaur and distinct from hadrosaurines.
Pascal Godefroit and colleagues argued in 1998 that skull material previously debated belonged to Bactrosaurus rather than Gilmoreosaurus.
Godefroit and colleagues concluded that the skull material belonged to Bactrosaurus, rejecting the idea of two taxa in the quarry.
